headline: SW Ledge's 9:10 slack: bass holding deep, first bonito flashing off Sandy Point
subhead: The rip window is shrinking to twenty minutes on either side of slack, but the fleet worked it hard enough to confirm the first bonito of the season off Block Island.
body_markdown:
The morning slack at SW Ledge has been running right around 9:10 this week, and that narrow stretch — call it twenty minutes before the turn and twenty after — has been the only reliable window worth fishing hard. Outside of it, the rip is either roaring too fast to hold a jig in the strike zone or it's dead flat with no current to push bait over the structure. That's a function of the moon building toward full, which is stacking more water through the Ledge on both the flood and the ebb and compressing the good fishing into tighter blocks. If you're planning a trip off Galilee this week, build the day around that slack, not the other way around.

Surface water is sitting in the high 60s to low 70s across the region — Kings Point up in the Sound reading 70.9, New London a touch cooler at 69.4, and Montauk holding 69.1 off to the west. That's warm enough to push striped bass into the classic late-August pattern: they're not gone, they're just not stupid. Daytime bites have gone quiet on the flats and open structure, and the better fish are sliding down onto the deeper edges of SW Ledge and the drop-offs east of the Point where there's still a cooler layer of water underneath the warm cap. Night tides and the gray light around dawn and dusk are outproducing the middle of the day by a wide margin right now, and that's not likely to change until the nights start cooling off in a couple weeks.

On the bonito — we flagged this last week, said Point Judith and Block Island would be among the first spots in the region to see them, and the fleet is now confirming fish showing off Sandy Point and along the rip lines north of North Light. They're still scattered and the window is short, but small pods have been popping bait on the surface in the first hour of daylight, chasing peanut bunker and rain bait that's been getting pushed tight against the beach by the current. Epoxy jigs in the 1-ounce range, small Deadly Dicks, and green-and-white Albie Snax on light spinning gear have been the go-to when the fish show — the mistake anglers keep making is throwing too big a profile at fish that are eating something the size of your pinky finger. Expect this pattern to build over the next week to ten days as more bonito filter in behind the bunker schools and water temps hold in this range.

Striped bass fishing itself has been a mixed bag, and it's worth being straight about that. The daytime bite on structure around SW Ledge has been spotty — a fish or two on a diamond jig worked slow along bottom in 40 to 60 feet on the last of the ebb, then long stretches of nothing. The better action has shifted to the night program, with eel-and-bucktail combinations and swimming plugs worked slow over the rocky stretches off Sandy Point and Clay Head after dark producing better numbers and better size. This is a summer holding pattern, not the start of the fall run — that push doesn't really get going until nighttime temperatures drop hard in mid-September, so there's no need to panic if the daytime bite feels thin right now. Patience and a headlamp are doing more work than a bigger boat.

Fluke have been the most disappointing story of the month, and the warm water is the reason. Fish have spread out across the open bottom instead of holding tight anywhere, which has softened catch rates everywhere except the channel edges and deeper humps where a cooler bottom layer survives. The better fluke this week have come from the deeper water off the Ledge and around the deeper cuts near Block Island, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Don't expect a bag limit — expect a keeper or two mixed with a lot of shorts if you're patient and stay on structure rather than drifting open sand.

Bluefish have been the one dependable player in the mix. Snapper blues are thick in Galilee's back channels and around the breachway, and cocktail-sized blues in the 3- to 6-pound range are showing up mixed into both the fluke drift and the striper program on structure, occasionally sawing through leaders meant for bass. Not glamorous, but steady, and a fine option for anyone who wants bent rods without needing the tide to line up perfectly.

Sea bass remain a solid secondary catch for anyone working the deeper wrecks and rock piles off the Point — nothing spectacular, but consistent numbers on squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs for boats willing to run a little farther and fish bottom instead of chasing the surface bite.

Looking ahead, expect the wind to stay out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 knot range through the next couple days, keeping the water clean and the SW Ledge slack fishable on schedule. As the moon fills out, tidal swings will keep sharpening, which should tighten up both the bass bite on structure and the bonito windows along the beaches. The real story to watch is temperature — once overnight lows start dropping into September, look for the daytime striper bite to wake back up on structure and for bonito numbers to build steadily rather than trickle in. For now, work the slack, fish it hard and short, and don't be surprised if the best fish of the week come after the sun goes down.
